read.sections.0.heading.source: It learns patterns from huge amounts of text
read.sections.0.heading.back: It learns patterns from a very large amount of text

read.sections.0.text.source: A chatbot is a computer program that you can chat with in writing. Many chatbots today are built on a large language model, or LLM. An LLM learns from a huge amount of text, such as books, articles and web pages. Much of it was written by people. From it, the model learns patterns, for example which words often come after other words. It works with small pieces of text, called tokens. A token may be a word or part of a word. Look at the made-up word game at Lakeside Learning Centre. After “a cup of”, its practice sentences had “tea” six times, “water” three times and “rice” once.
read.sections.0.text.back: A chatbot is a computer program you can chat with in writing. Many chatbots today are built on a large language model, or LLM. An LLM learns from a very large amount of text, such as books, articles and web pages. Most of it was written by people. From that text, the model learns patterns, for example words that often come after other words. It works with small bits of text, called tokens. One token may be one word or part of a word. Look at the invented word game at Lakeside Learning Centre. After “a cup of”, its practice sentences had “tea” six times, “water” three times and “rice” once.
read.sections.0.text.note: "Small pieces of text" is "cebisan teks" throughout. "Chat with" is "ajak bersembang".

read.sections.0.simpler.source: A chatbot is a program you can chat with. Many chatbots use a large language model, or LLM. An LLM learns from lots of text, like books and web pages. People wrote much of it. The LLM finds patterns in the words. It works with tokens. A token is a word or part of a word. In the Lakeside word game, “tea” came most often after “a cup of”.
read.sections.0.simpler.back: A chatbot is a program you can chat with. Many chatbots use a large language model, or LLM. An LLM learns from a lot of text, like books and web pages. People wrote most of it. The LLM looks for patterns in the words. It works with tokens. A token is one word or part of a word. In the Lakeside word game, “tea” came most often after “a cup of”.

read.sections.1.heading.source: It writes one piece at a time
read.sections.1.heading.back: It writes one bit at a time

read.sections.1.text.source: When you ask an LLM a question, it predicts the next token of its answer, adds it, and predicts the one after it, again and again. Often each token is picked partly by chance from the likely ones, so the Lakeside model would often say “tea”, but sometimes “water”. With other settings, a model can give the same answer every time. Chatbots are not new: in 1966, a program called ELIZA chatted by following rules that people wrote. LLMs use machine learning instead. In 2017, researchers published a new design for language tasks. ChatGPT, released on 30 November 2022, made LLMs famous.
read.sections.1.text.back: When you ask an LLM a question, it predicts the next token in its answer, adds it, and predicts the token after that, again and again. Usually each token is chosen partly at random from the likely tokens, so the Lakeside model would usually say “tea”, but sometimes “water”. With other settings, a model can give the same answer every time. Chatbots are not new: in 1966, a program named ELIZA chatted by following rules written by people. LLMs, however, use machine learning. In 2017, researchers published a new design for language tasks. ChatGPT, launched on 30 November 2022, made LLMs famous.
read.sections.1.text.note: "Partly by chance" is "sebahagiannya secara rawak" (partly at random), matching "random" in the sources and teachers' notes.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: You ask an LLM a question. It predicts the next token, again and again. Often it picks partly by chance. So the Lakeside model often says “tea”, but sometimes “water”. With other settings, it gives the same answer each time. Chatbots are not new. In 1966, one followed rules that people wrote. LLMs learn from examples instead. Researchers made a new design in 2017. In November 2022, ChatGPT made them famous.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: You ask an LLM a question. It predicts the next token, again and again. Usually it chooses partly at random. read.sections.2.heading.source: Sounding sure is not the same as being right
read.sections.2.heading.back: Sounding confident is not the same as being right

read.sections.2.text.source: A basic LLM predicts words that sound right. It does not check facts the way a careful person does. So it can make things up, and it can sound very confident even when it is wrong. At Lakeside, the pretend helper named a book that does not exist. Some tools also search the web and show links, but the pages can be wrong or misread, so you still need to check them. Most big LLMs learned mainly from English text, and researchers have found they work worse in languages with little writing online. So check important answers with a trusted source, such as a library or a teacher.

write.example.source: A large language model learns from a huge amount of text, much of it written by people. It writes an answer by predicting the next token, a word or part of a word, again and again. It can be useful for explaining ideas or translating short notices. But it can be wrong because it picks words that sound right. It does not check facts. At Lakeside, the helper named a book that does not exist, and it sounded sure. watch.summary.source: In this video, two people who build AI tools explain how chatbots work. One works at the company that made ChatGPT. A large language model learns from a huge amount of text from the internet. The main idea is simple. It uses numbers about what is likely, worked out very fast. The video shows a small example. A program reads plays by the writer Shakespeare. It counts which letter often comes after each letter. When it writes this way, the words look strange. When it looks at longer pieces, like whole words, its guesses get much better. Big models use neural networks, which are loosely based on the brain. People also helped to make ChatGPT's answers better. But its answers still come from what is likely, so it can make mistakes.
watch.summary.back: In this video, two people who build AI tools explain how chatbots work. One of them works at the company that made ChatGPT. A large language model learns from a very large amount of text from the internet. The main idea is simple. It uses numbers about what is likely, calculated very fast. The video shows one small example. A program reads plays by the writer Shakespeare. It counts the letters that often come after each letter. When it writes this way, the words look strange. When it looks at longer bits, like whole words, its guesses become much better. Big models use neural networks, which are loosely based on the brain. People also helped make ChatGPT's answers better. But its answers still come from what is likely, so it can make mistakes.

educatorNotes.0.source: There is no real chatbot in the app (docs/content/DIGITAL_WORLD_SPEC.md 5.6). The Lakeside word game, the helper's answers and the book “The Long Blue Road” are made up. The cup-of-tea game is a toy analogy, not a full account: real LLMs work on tokens and far more text, and the lesson's “word” is a simplification. Not all training text is written by people (some models also learn from computer-made text), so the lesson says “much of it”. A model can repeat an answer: an app can pick the likeliest token every time, or pick at random among likely ones (Google's course).
educatorNotes.0.back: There is no real chatbot in this app (docs/content/DIGITAL_WORLD_SPEC.md 5.6). The Lakeside word game, the helper's answers and the book “The Long Blue Road” are invented. The cup-of-tea game is a simple analogy, not a complete explanation: real LLMs work with tokens and far more text, and the “word” in this lesson is a simplification. Not all training text is written by people (some models also learn from computer-made text), so this lesson says “most of it”. A model can repeat an answer: an app can choose the most likely token every time, or choose at random among likely tokens (Google's course).

educatorNotes.1.source: A basic model writes from what it learned; some tools also search the web and show links. A link is not proof: open it and check it, as in Lesson 14 (Stanford CRAFT's lesson on fact-checking AI search results). The 2017 design is the transformer (Vaswani and others). Paper version of the activity: write the nine sentences on cards and sort them into “Can”, “Can't” and “Hard to say”; reward reasons.
educatorNotes.1.back: A basic model writes from what it has learned; some tools also search the web and show links. A link is not proof: open and check that link, as in Lesson 14 (Stanford CRAFT's lesson on fact-checking AI search results). The 2017 design is the transformer (Vaswani and colleagues). Paper version of this activity: write the nine sentences on cards and sort them into “Can”, “Cannot” and “Hard to say”; value the reasons given.
educatorNotes.1.note: The paper sort's three group names are "Boleh", "Tidak boleh" and "Sukar dikatakan", short forms of the activity's groups.
